newsitem.title: FINLAND: JOBS-Nordic jobless rates may heighten EMU doubts.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-Nordic jobless rates may heighten EMU doubts.

text.p: There are much worse places to be on the dole than the Nordic countries: welfare offers safety nets for jobless men and women alike, and in some countries also helps massage the figures to relatively undramatic levels.

But even if high joblessness does not look likely to trigger mass street protest from organised and well cared-for Swedes, Danes and Finns, it is increasingly -- even only by association -- bringing Europe's single currency plans into question.

That issue is most apparent in Sweden, where unions and labour authorities are urging the Social Democrat-led government to prioritise job creation over any economic hoop that countries must jump through to qualify for Economic and Monetary Union.
Sweden's Labour Market Board AMS recently recommended that Sweden wait before joining EMU on the grounds of high unemployment.
"Unemployment is too high," said AMS spokesman Mats Klingvall. "It would be sad if it were to rise without us being able to counteract it with every conceivable means."
He was talking about a country where the official jobless rate, at 8.8 percent in January, is at record high levels but still about half the comparable rate in its eastern neighbour, Finland.

Ironically an east-west tour of the Nordic countries -- from Finland to Norway -- starts with the highest jobless rate and firmest government resolve to join the single currency, and ends in the country with most people in work, but outside the EU.

Again by association, that alone could fuel populist opposition to a single currency in coming months. If it were combined with sustained similar signals from EMU-engine Germany, it may undermine political commitment to the project.
FINNS SET FOR DOLE IN EUROS?
Finland, which for decades enjoyed near full employment, was hit hard by the early 1990s recession after the Soviet Union collapsed, slashing its exports to the east almost to nil.
Joblessness surged from four percent to 20 percent in three years. It is now inching down but remains stubbornly high and at nearly 17 percent in January was second-highest in the European Union.
Finland now is also one of few EU countries both likely and willing to meet criteria for a single currency: its Social Democrat-led government is committed to joining the first wave.
Building on Nordic welfare tradition, Finland has let social costs rise, financing deficits by hefty borrowing.
The strategy has had some success: generous welfare has helped calm and occupy the jobless.
But the disincentives to work created by the system have boosted the grey economy and may hinder growth.
The government, which vowed when it took office to halve unemployment to eight or nine percent by the end of its term in 1999, plans to cut income taxes to make work more rewarding.
But it has recently acknowledged its jobless bid may fail, although it says strong growth -- forecast at almost five percent this year -- will help tackle unemployment to 1999.
One area the government is not expected to cut is unemployment benefit, because it would face stiff opposition from unions whose support it may need to get Finland into EMU.

That leaves the labour market with a structural problem: to boost net earnings by just 25 percent, an unemployed person would need a job with almost 60 percent higher gross pay than they are getting in jobless benefits.
SWEDES ALREADY DOUBTING
Swedish unemployment at nearly nine percent has in the past five years surged to levels unheard of in modern times: from the fifties to most of the eighties, it was below three percent.

In Sweden data is also available on "real" or "total" unemployment -- including the hidden jobless in government work schemes -- which in January totalled 15 percent, almost level with the official Finnish figure.
Like Finnish leaders, the minority government has promised to halve official unemployment to the year 2000, but so far nothing has happened.
Analysts and economists doubt its ability to do much about total unemployment but say it could succeed in cutting the official figures by shuffling more people into schemes.

Unemployment is hampering a pick-up in the sluggish home economy, as people worried about job security choose saving over spending, and is already an explicit barrier to joining the euro first wave: unions worried about it have turned against EMU.
The Social Democrats, also traditionally supported by the unions, are still undecided on the single currency.
DANES ALREADY SAID NO TO EMU, BUT JOBLESS COST
Unlike some neighbours, Denmark has no need of "austerity" programmes to meet single currency criteria -- it already qualifies and, in any case, Danes voted against EMU in a binding 1993 referendum.

Comparable to Sweden, Denmark's official unemployment rate of 8.8 percent for 1996 is forecast to fall to 7.6 percent in 1998, reducing government spending on the welfare system but raising the danger of upward wage pressure.

However, most analysts estimate that the real number of people off work is at least double the official figure, masked by myriad paid leave and job creation schemes, retraining programmes and early retirement.

The high level of female participation in the labour force in Denmark and other Nordic countries means such estimates are likely to be quite close to reality: Danish figures show about 75 percent of women of working age have or are seeking jobs.
Cost is the main headache. A 1996 government guide put welfare expenditure in 1992 at 30 percent of GNP.
The maximum rate of unemployment benefit is 90 percent of previous income up to a ceiling around $21,000 a year, for a maximum of five years.

The government -- also led by Social Democrats, due to fight for re-election next year -- has pledged both to bring down joblessness and get the public sector budget, currently in the red, back into surplus in 1997.
SOME MAY FIND WORK IN NORWAY

Oil-rich Norway, undergoing a strong upturn after stagnating in the late 1980s, is one of few European countries to show a budget surplus -- estimated this year around 14 percent of total spending, statistics officials say.
Today it has one of the highest rates of employment growth among the OECD countries and one of the lowest jobless rates: between four and five percent, depending on the source.
But there are signs of a growing mismatch of labour skills, especially in healthcare and construction, and the west of the country is short of skilled shipbuilding workers.
Norway usually looks to its Scandinavian neighbours to fill vacant positions, mainly because of similarities in language.
But its labour costs rose last year, fuelled also by higher profitability in manufacturing. Longer term, this could lead to a loss of competitiveness and a negative impact on employment.
Again ironically, that points back to the theoretical potential of the euro.
